The biojava-survival module provides a comprehensive Java implementation of key survival analysis techniques, including **Cox proportional hazards regression** and **Kaplan-Meier survival estimation**, making these powerful statistical methods accessible to Java developers working with biological and clinical data.

## Understanding Survival Analysis in Bioinformatics

Survival analysis deals with analyzing data where the outcome is the time until the occurrence of an event of interest. In bioinformatics, this could be time until death, disease recurrence, or treatment failure. What makes survival analysis unique is its ability to handle **censored data** - cases where we don't know the exact event time because the event hasn't occurred yet or the subject was lost to follow-up.

The biojava-survival module implements two fundamental approaches:

1. **Kaplan-Meier Estimation**: A non-parametric method used to estimate the survival function from lifetime data
2. **Cox Proportional Hazards Model**: A semi-parametric regression model for analyzing the effect of multiple variables on survival time

Sources: [CoxMethod.java#L27-L36](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/CoxMethod.java#L27-L36), [SurvFitKM.java#L44-L50](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/kaplanmeier/figure/SurvFitKM.java#L44-L50)

## Module Architecture and Key Components

The biojava-survival module is organized into three main packages, each serving a specific purpose in the survival analysis workflow:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[biojava-survival] --> B[cox]
    A --> C[data]
    A --> D[kaplanmeier]
    
    B --> B1[CoxR.java]
    B --> B2[CoxHelper.java]
    B --> B3[SurvivalInfo.java]
    
    C --> C1[WorkSheet.java]
    C --> C2[HeaderInfo.java]
    
    D --> D1[KaplanMeierFigure.java]
    D --> D2[SurvFitKM.java]
```

### Core Data Structures

At the heart of the module are two key data structures:

**SurvivalInfo**: Represents individual survival data points with essential information:
- `time`: The survival time or censoring time
- `status`: Event indicator (1=event occurred, 0=censored)
- `data`: LinkedHashMap containing covariates and their values
- Additional fields for weights, strata, and cluster information

**WorkSheet**: A memory-efficient data structure for handling large datasets, similar to a spreadsheet but optimized for performance with biological data.

Sources: [SurvivalInfo.java#L34-L54](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/SurvivalInfo.java#L34-L54), [WorkSheet.java#L32-L38](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/data/WorkSheet.java#L32-L38)

## Getting Started with Cox Regression

The Cox proportional hazards model is the most widely used regression model for survival analysis. It allows you to examine the effect of multiple variables on survival time without needing to specify the underlying survival distribution.

### Basic Cox Regression Analysis

Here's how to perform a simple Cox regression analysis using the CoxHelper class:

```java
// Load survival data from a tab-delimited file
String dataFile = "path/to/your/data.txt";
String timeColumn = "TIME";
String statusColumn = "CENSOR";
String[] variables = {"AGE", "TREATMENT", "RACE"};

// Perform Cox regression
CoxHelper coxHelper = new CoxHelper();
CoxInfo coxInfo = coxHelper.process(dataFile, timeColumn, statusColumn, 
                                   "", "", "", variables, false, false);

// Get results
double[] coefficients = coxInfo.getCoefficients();
double[] pValues = coxInfo.getPValues();
```

The results include:
- **Coefficients**: Log hazard ratios for each variable
- **P-values**: Statistical significance of each variable
- **Confidence intervals**: Range of plausible values for hazard ratios
- **Model fit statistics**: Overall model performance measures

Sources: [CoxHelper.java#L29-L50](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/CoxHelper.java#L29-L50), [uis-complete.txt#L1-L20](biojava-survival/src/main/resources/uis-complete.txt#L1-L20)

### Advanced Cox Regression Features

The module supports advanced features for more sophisticated analyses:

```java
// Cox regression with strata and weights
CoxInfo coxInfo = coxHelper.process(dataFile, timeColumn, statusColumn,
                                   "WEIGHT", "STRATA", "", variables, true, true);

// Using different methods for handling tied events
CoxMethod method = CoxMethod.Efron; // or CoxMethod.Breslow
CoxR coxR = new CoxR();
coxR.process(survivalDataList, method, maxIterations, tolerance);
```

> [!TIP]
> The choice between Breslow and Efron methods depends on your data. Breslow is faster but less accurate when many events occur at the same time. Efron provides better accuracy for tied events but requires more computational resources.

Sources: [CoxMethod.java#L27-L36](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/CoxMethod.java#L27-L36), [CoxR.java#L33-L42](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/CoxR.java#L33-L42)

## Kaplan-Meier Survival Analysis

Kaplan-Meier analysis is used to estimate and visualize survival curves, showing the probability of survival over time for different groups.

### Creating Survival Curves

```java
// Prepare survival data
ArrayList<SurvivalInfo> survivalData = new ArrayList<>();
survivalData.add(new SurvivalInfo(10, 1, "GROUP", 1)); // time=10, event=1, group=1
survivalData.add(new SurvivalInfo(15, 0, "GROUP", 1)); // time=15, censored=0, group=1
survivalData.add(new SurvivalInfo(8, 1, "GROUP", 2));  // time=8, event=1, group=2

// Perform Kaplan-Meier analysis
SurvFitKM survFit = new SurvFitKM();
SurvFitInfo survFitInfo = survFit.process(survivalData, "GROUP");

// Create visualization
KaplanMeierFigure kmFigure = new KaplanMeierFigure();
kmFigure.generateFigure(survFitInfo, "Survival Analysis by Treatment Group");
```

### Interpreting Kaplan-Meier Curves

The Kaplan-Meier figure shows:
- **Y-axis**: Survival probability (from 1.0 to 0.0)
- **X-axis**: Time
- **Steps**: Drops indicate events (deaths/failures)
- **Tick marks**: Indicate censored observations
- **Multiple curves**: Different groups can be compared on the same plot

Sources: [KaplanMeierFigure.java#L41-L50](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/kaplanmeier/figure/KaplanMeierFigure.java#L41-L50), [SurvFitKM.java#L34-L38](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/kaplanmeier/figure/SurvFitKM.java#L34-L38)

## Data Preparation and Best Practices

### Working with Clinical Data

The module includes example data in `uis-complete.txt` that demonstrates the typical format for survival analysis:

```
ID	AGE	BECKTOTA	HERCOC	IVHX	NDRUGTX	RACE	TREAT	SITE	LOS	TIME	CENSOR
101	33	.	.	.	6	0	1	0	2	2	1
152	22	.	.	.	3	0	1	0	3	3	1
```

Key columns for survival analysis:
- **TIME**: Survival time or time to event
- **CENSOR**: Event indicator (1=event, 0=censored)
- **Other columns**: Covariates for analysis

### Data Quality Considerations

When preparing data for survival analysis:

1. **Handle missing values**: The module can handle missing data (marked as ".")
2. **Ensure proper time units**: Consistent time units across all observations
3. **Verify censoring status**: Correct coding of events vs. censored observations
4. **Check for outliers**: Extreme values can significantly affect results

Sources: [uis-complete.txt#L1-L20](biojava-survival/src/main/resources/uis-complete.txt#L1-L20), [SurvivalInfo.java#L60-L96](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/SurvivalInfo.java#L60-L96)

## Internal Architecture and Performance

The biojava-survival module is designed for performance with large biological datasets:

### Memory Optimization

- **CompactCharSequence**: Used in WorkSheet to minimize memory footprint
- **Efficient data structures**: LinkedHashMap for fast lookups while maintaining order
- **Stream processing**: Large files can be processed without loading everything into memory

### Algorithm Implementation

The Cox regression implementation is a port of R's survival package, adapted for Java's object-oriented paradigm:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant CoxHelper
    participant CoxR
    participant SurvivalInfo
    participant Matrix
    
    User->>CoxHelper: process(dataFile, columns)
    CoxHelper->>WorkSheet: load data
    CoxHelper->>SurvivalInfo: create objects
    CoxHelper->>CoxR: process data
    CoxR->>Matrix: perform calculations
    CoxR->>CoxR: iterative optimization
    CoxR-->>CoxHelper: return CoxInfo
    CoxHelper-->>User: return results
```

The algorithm uses:
- **Newton-Raphson optimization**: For finding maximum likelihood estimates
- **Cholesky decomposition**: For matrix operations in variance calculations
- **Efficient handling of ties**: Both Breslow and Efron methods implemented

Sources: [CoxR.java#L53-L95](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/CoxR.java#L53-L95), [WorkSheet.java#L26-L38](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/data/WorkSheet.java#L26-L38)

## Integration with Other BioJava Modules

The survival analysis module can be integrated with other BioJava components for comprehensive bioinformatics analysis:

### Combining with Structure Analysis

```java
// Analyze protein structure features and survival
ProteinStructure structure = StructureIO.getStructure("protein.pdb");
double stabilityScore = calculateStability(structure);

// Add to survival data
SurvivalInfo survInfo = new SurvivalInfo(survivalTime, eventStatus);
survInfo.getData().put("PROTEIN_STABILITY", stabilityScore);
```

### Integration with Sequence Analysis

```java
// Analyze sequence features and correlate with survival
DNASequence sequence = new DNASequence(dnaString);
double gcContent = sequence.getGCContent();

SurvivalInfo survInfo = new SurvivalInfo(survivalTime, eventStatus);
survInfo.getData().put("GC_CONTENT", gcContent);
```

This integration allows researchers to investigate relationships between molecular features and clinical outcomes, enabling precision medicine applications.

> [!TIP]
> When integrating multiple data types, ensure proper normalization of features. Different scales (e.g., protein stability scores vs. gene expression levels) can affect model convergence and interpretation.

Sources: [pom.xml#L21-L50](biojava-survival/pom.xml#L21-L50), [SurvivalInfo.java#L48-L54](biojava-survival/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/survival/cox/SurvivalInfo.java#L48-L54)

## Conclusion

The biojava-survival module provides a robust, Java-based implementation of essential survival analysis methods. By offering both Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier analysis with comprehensive visualization capabilities, it enables bioinformaticians to:

1. **Analyze time-to-event data** with proper handling of censored observations
2. **Identify prognostic factors** using multivariate Cox regression
3. **Visualize survival patterns** with publication-ready Kaplan-Meier curves
4. **Integrate molecular data** with clinical outcomes for biomarker discovery

Whether you're analyzing clinical trial data, studying disease progression, or investigating the relationship between molecular features and patient outcomes, the biojava-survival module provides the statistical tools needed for rigorous survival analysis in a Java environment.

The module's efficient implementation, comprehensive feature set, and integration capabilities make it a valuable addition to any bioinformatician's toolkit for survival analysis applications.

# Extending BioJava



BioJava is designed as a modular framework that provides a solid foundation for bioinformatics applications while allowing developers to extend its functionality to meet specific research needs. This document explores how you can leverage BioJava's architecture to build custom features and integrate them seamlessly with the existing framework.

## Understanding BioJava's Modular Architecture

BioJava is organized as a multi-module Maven project where each module addresses specific aspects of bioinformatics. The framework follows a layered architecture with the core module providing fundamental abstractions and specialized modules building upon this foundation.

The main modules include:
- **biojava-core**: Provides fundamental classes for sequences, compounds, and basic operations
- **biojava-alignment**: Implements sequence alignment algorithms
- **biojava-structure**: Handles protein structure representation and analysis
- **biojava-genome**: Offers genome-scale analysis capabilities
- **biojava-ontology**: Supports biological ontology management
- And several other specialized modules

This modular design allows you to:
1. Use only the modules relevant to your application
2. Extend specific functionality without affecting the entire system
3. Create new modules that integrate seamlessly with existing ones

Sources: [pom.xml#L637-L651](pom.xml#L637-L651)

## Core Extension Points

The biojava-core module provides several key extension points that serve as the foundation for building custom functionality. Understanding these abstractions is crucial for effective extension.

### Sequence and Compound Framework

The sequence framework in BioJava is built around template interfaces that allow for flexible implementations. The core interfaces include:

- `Sequence`: Represents a biological sequence with methods for accessing compounds, length, and metadata
- `Compound`: Represents individual elements in a sequence (nucleotides, amino acids, etc.)
- `SequenceReader`: Allows for reading sequences from various sources
- `SequenceWriter`: Enables writing sequences to different formats

These interfaces are designed to be extended for specialized biological sequences or compounds not directly supported by BioJava.

```java
public class CustomSequence extends AbstractSequence<CustomCompound> {
    
    public CustomSequence(List<CustomCompound> compounds) {
        super(compounds);
    }
    
    @Override
    public String getSequenceAsString() {
        // Custom implementation
    }
    
    // Additional custom methods
}
```

Sources: [biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/sequence/template/](biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/sequence/template/)

### Data Parsers and Writers

BioJava provides a flexible I/O framework that can be extended to support new file formats. The core includes:

- `SequenceReaderInterface`: For implementing custom sequence parsers
- `SequenceWriterInterface`: For implementing custom sequence writers
- `ProxySequenceReader`: A wrapper class that can be extended for custom data sources

To implement a custom parser, you would extend the appropriate interface and implement the required methods:

```java
public class CustomFormatParser implements SequenceReaderInterface<ProteinSequence, AminoAcidCompound> {
    
    @Override
    public ProteinSequence readSequence(BufferedReader reader) throws IOException {
        // Parse custom format and return sequence
    }
    
    @Override
    public Map<String, ProteinSequence> processMultiple(BufferedReader reader) throws IOException {
        // Handle multiple sequences in custom format
    }
}
```

Sources: [biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/sequence/io/](biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/sequence/io/)

## Creating Custom Modules

When your extensions become substantial, creating a new BioJava module is the best approach. This ensures proper integration with the BioJava ecosystem and follows the established patterns.

### Module Structure

A new BioJava module should follow the standard Maven project structure:

```
biojava-myfeature/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    ├── main/
    │   ├── java/
    │   └── resources/
    └── test/
        ├── java/
        └── resources/
```

The `pom.xml` for your module should inherit from the main BioJava POM and declare dependencies on the required BioJava modules:

```xml
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0" xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 http://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
    
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.biojava</groupId>
        <artifactId>biojava</artifactId>
        <version>7.2.3-SNAPSHOT</version>
    </parent>
    
    <artifactId>biojava-myfeature</artifactId>
    <name>biojava-myfeature</name>
    <description>Custom feature module for BioJava</description>
    
    <dependencies>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.biojava</groupId>
            <artifactId>biojava-core</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Add other required BioJava modules -->
    </dependencies>
</project>
```

Sources: [biojava-structure/pom.xml](biojava-structure/pom.xml)

### Registering Your Module

Once your module is created, you need to register it in the main BioJava POM by adding it to the modules section:

```xml
<modules>
    <!-- Existing modules -->
    <module>biojava-core</module>
    <module>biojava-alignment</module>
    <!-- ... -->
    
    <!-- Your new module -->
    <module>biojava-myfeature</module>
    
    <!-- Keep integration tests last -->
    <module>biojava-integrationtest</module>
</modules>
```

Sources: [pom.xml#L637-L651](pom.xml#L637-L651)

## Extending Structure Analysis

The biojava-structure module demonstrates how to build specialized functionality on top of the core. It provides classes for representing and analyzing protein 3D structures.

### Structure Representation

The structure module uses a hierarchical model:
- `Structure`: Represents the entire protein structure
- `Model`: Contains different conformational models
- `Chain`: Represents polypeptide chains
- `Group`: Represents amino acids or nucleotides
- `Atom`: Represents individual atoms

You can extend these classes to add custom properties or behaviors:

```java
public class CustomStructure extends StructureImpl {
    
    private Map<String, Object> customProperties;
    
    public void addCustomProperty(String key, Object value) {
        if (customProperties == null) {
            customProperties = new HashMap<>();
        }
        customProperties.put(key, value);
    }
    
    public Object getCustomProperty(String key) {
        return customProperties != null ? customProperties.get(key) : null;
    }
}
```

Sources: [biojava-structure/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/structure/StructureImpl.java](biojava-structure/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/structure/StructureImpl.java)

### Custom Structure Calculations

The structure module includes utility classes like `Calc` for common structural calculations. You can extend this pattern to add your own calculations:

```java
public class CustomStructureCalculations {
    
    public static double calculateCustomMetric(Structure structure) {
        // Implement custom structural analysis
        double result = 0.0;
        
        for (Chain chain : structure.getChains()) {
            for (Group group : chain.getAtomGroups()) {
                // Perform calculations
            }
        }
        
        return result;
    }
}
```

Sources: [biojava-structure/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/structure/Calc.java](biojava-structure/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/structure/Calc.java)

## Implementing Custom Algorithms

BioJava's design encourages the implementation of custom algorithms through well-defined interfaces and abstract classes.

### Algorithm Design Pattern

Most algorithms in BioJava follow a consistent pattern:
1. Define an interface for the algorithm
2. Provide an abstract base class with common functionality
3. Implement specific algorithms as concrete classes

For example, to implement a custom sequence alignment algorithm:

```java
public interface CustomAligner {
    AlignmentResult align(Sequence seq1, Sequence seq2);
}

public abstract class AbstractCustomAligner implements CustomAligner {
    protected SubstitutionMatrix matrix;
    protected GapPenalty gapPenalty;
    
    // Common functionality for all implementations
    protected void initialize(Sequence seq1, Sequence seq2) {
        // Initialization code
    }
}

public class MyCustomAligner extends AbstractCustomAligner {
    @Override
    public AlignmentResult align(Sequence seq1, Sequence seq2) {
        // Implement specific alignment algorithm
        initialize(seq1, seq2);
        // ... alignment logic
        return new AlignmentResult();
    }
}
```

Sources: [biojava-alignment/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/alignment/template/](biojava-alignment/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/alignment/template/)

## Contributing Extensions to BioJava

If you've developed an extension that could benefit the broader BioJava community, consider contributing it back to the project.

### Development Guidelines

1. **Follow Coding Standards**: BioJava uses specific coding standards documented in the development directory
2. **Write Tests**: Include comprehensive unit tests for your extensions
3. **Documentation**: Provide clear documentation for your extensions
4. **License Compliance**: Ensure your contributions comply with BioJava's LGPL v2 license

Sources: [development/HEADER.txt](development/HEADER.txt)

### Submission Process

1. Fork the BioJava repository on GitHub
2. Create a feature branch for your extension
3. Implement your extension following the established patterns
4. Add tests and documentation
5. Submit a pull request for review

The BioJava team reviews contributions based on:
- Technical merit and correctness
- Consistency with existing codebase
- Documentation quality
- Test coverage

Sources: [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md)

> [!TIP]
> When extending BioJava, always prefer implementing interfaces over extending concrete classes. This approach provides better flexibility and makes your code more resilient to changes in the BioJava framework.

## Best Practices for Extending BioJava

To ensure your extensions are robust and maintainable, follow these best practices:

### 1. Leverage Existing Abstractions

```java
// Good: Use template interfaces
public class CustomSequenceReader implements SequenceReaderInterface<ProteinSequence, AminoAcidCompound> {
    // Implementation
}

// Avoid: Extending concrete implementations
public class CustomSequenceReader extends FastaSequenceReader {
    // This may break if FastaSequenceReader changes
}
```

### 2. Handle Exceptions Appropriately

BioJava defines specific exception types for different scenarios. Use these in your extensions:

```java
public void processSequence(Sequence sequence) throws CompoundNotFoundException {
    // Check for invalid compounds
    if (sequence == null) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Sequence cannot be null");
    }
    
    // Process sequence
}
```

Sources: [biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/exceptions/](biojava-core/src/main/java/org/biojava/nbio/core/exceptions/)

### 3. Use Logging Framework

BioJava uses SLF4J with Log4j2 for logging. Integrate with this framework in your extensions:

```java
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

public class CustomProcessor {
    private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(CustomProcessor.class);
    
    public void process(Sequence sequence) {
        logger.info("Processing sequence: {}", sequence.getAccession());
        // Processing logic
        logger.debug("Processing completed successfully");
    }
}
```

Sources: [biojava-core/pom.xml#L39-L41](biojava-core/pom.xml#L39-L41)

### 4. Follow Package Conventions

BioJava organizes code into logical packages. Follow these conventions in your extensions:

- `org.biojava.nbio.core.*`: Core abstractions and interfaces
- `org.biojava.nbio.structure.*`: Structure-related functionality
- `org.biojava.nbio.alignment.*`: Alignment algorithms
- `org.biojava.nbio.genome.*`: Genome analysis tools

## Conclusion

Extending BioJava is a powerful way to customize the framework for your specific bioinformatics needs. By understanding the modular architecture and following the established patterns, you can create robust extensions that integrate seamlessly with the BioJava ecosystem.

Whether you're implementing custom algorithms, adding support for new data formats, or creating entirely new modules, BioJava's extensible design provides the flexibility you need while maintaining compatibility with the broader framework.

Remember to leverage the existing abstractions, follow the coding standards, and consider contributing your extensions back to the community to help advance bioinformatics research for everyone.
